subject: Feature superposition density as a function of layer depth and its implications for probing classifier reliability

Topic: Feature superposition density as a function of layer depth and its implications for probing classifier reliability

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-796)
response:
Feature superposition density refers to how many linearly independent "features" (directions in activation space corresponding to recognizable semantic or functional concepts) a given layer appears to pack into its residual stream or MLP hidden dimension — and how that packing density changes as you move from early to late layers. The central question is whether probing classifiers trained on intermediate-layer activations are actually detecting cleanly represented features, or whether they're detecting linear readouts of superposed features that may partially overlap, rotate, or shift across the forward pass. The key concepts are: the superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al. 2022), which holds that networks store more features than dimensions by tolerating interference; polysemanticity (individual neurons responding to multiple unrelated features); and probing reliability, which asks whether a probe's accuracy reflects the model's actual internal representation or an artifact of how superposed features happen to project onto the probe's training distribution.

What a beginner misses is that probe accuracy is not evidence of clean representation. A probe can achieve 90% accuracy on a concept while the underlying direction is entangled with three other features — the probe is essentially fitting the dominant term in a superposition, and any downstream conclusion about "what the model knows at layer N" is then contaminated by the geometry of that entanglement. Experts worry specifically that superposition density is not monotonic with depth: early layers tend to be sparse and polysemantic in specific ways (edge/token-level features), middle layers may be the most densely superposed (many abstract features, limited dimensionality), and late layers re-specialize for output-relevant directions — meaning probe reliability has a non-trivial depth profile that most probing studies ignore by picking a single layer.

NEXT: If superposition density peaks in middle layers, what experimental signature would distinguish "the probe is fitting a clean feature that happens to coexist with others" from "the probe is fitting an interference artifact with no stable causal role"?

The sharpest experimental signature is causal intervention under targeted suppression: if you ablate or clamp the probed direction (via activation patching or a rank-1 update to the weight matrices) and the predicted behavior changes in the expected direction, the feature has causal standing; if behavior is unchanged or changes in an unrelated way, the probe was fitting interference. Hernandez et al. (2023) on "linear representations" and the broader activation patching literature (Wang et al., IOI circuit, 2022) operationalize exactly this — patching a direction that a probe identifies as "subject token binding" in GPT-2 small produces the predicted logit shifts, lending causal credibility. The complementary signature is cross-context stability: a clean feature should probe with consistent accuracy across semantically diverse prompt distributions that hold the concept fixed but vary surrounding context; an interference artifact will show probe accuracy that degrades sharply when the prompt distribution shifts, because the artifact depends on correlated co-activations in the training distribution rather than the concept itself. A third, more geometric test is whether the probed direction is sparse in the neuron basis (as measured by the L1/L0 weight profile of the probe or by dictionary learning methods like Cunningham et al. 2023's sparse autoencoders on MLP layers of GPT-2) — clean features recovered by SAEs tend to have interpretable, stable activating examples, while interference artifacts produce incoherent top-activating inputs. The worry experts carry is that all three tests can give false positives simultaneously if the "artifact" is a stable interference pattern — a consistent linear combination of real features that the model reliably produces in a broad context class, making it behaviorally potent even though it isn't atomic.

The honest answer is that there are no guarantees — the SAE objective (reconstruct activations with sparse codes) is entirely agnostic to causal atomicity, and a dictionary that achieves low reconstruction loss with high sparsity could in principle consist entirely of stable interference patterns that happen to be frequently co-activated. The closest thing to a theoretical grounding comes from the linear representation hypothesis itself: if the model's loss landscape genuinely incentivizes storing features as approximately orthogonal directions (the core claim in Elhage et al. 2022's toy model analysis), then SAE recovery should approximately converge to causally meaningful directions — but this argument is circular when applied to middle layers where we don't independently know the feature geometry. Empirically, Cunningham et al. (2023) validated some SAE features by showing that their top-activating dataset examples are humanly coherent (e.g., a "DNA sequence" feature fires on genetic text), and Bricken et al. (2023) on one-layer MLP features in Claude found that clamping individual SAE features produces interpretable downstream effects — but both validations rely on human coherence and single-feature ablations, neither of which rules out the feature being a compressed representation of a feature cluster rather than an atom. The deeper problem is identifiability: the mapping from activation space to sparse codes is underdetermined up to rotations within the active set, meaning two SAEs trained with different random seeds or slightly different sparsity penalties can recover geometrically distinct dictionaries with equivalent reconstruction loss — Anthropic's own scaling experiments (Templeton et al. 2024) note feature splitting across dictionary sizes, where a "feature" at 512 dimensions splits into 4-6 more specific features at 4096, which implies the 512-dimensional version was never atomic to begin with. What experts find most troubling is that the standard evaluation pipeline — train SAE, inspect top activating examples, ablate, conclude atomicity — has no step that checks whether the recovered direction is minimal in the causal sense, i.e., whether it can be further decomposed into causally independent sub-directions that the SAE merged due to insufficient dictionary size or sparsity pressure.

There is no principled stopping criterion derivable from first principles, and the feature-splitting phenomenon itself suggests atomicity may be a scale-relative rather than absolute property — what counts as a feature depends on the resolution at which you're asking causal questions. The best candidate for a stopping criterion would be a causal closure condition: a dictionary size D* at which further expansion produces new directions whose ablation effects are entirely predictable as linear combinations of ablation effects from the D*-sized dictionary — but no one has operationalized this test at scale, and it would require an exponential number of combinatorial ablations to verify rigorously. Templeton et al. (2024) observed splitting ratios of roughly 4-6x between adjacent dictionary scales in Claude's MLP layers, with no sign of convergence at the largest tested sizes (up to ~1M features), which is empirically consistent with the interpretation that the model's "true" feature count either exceeds any tractable dictionary or that the concept of a terminal atomic feature is simply not well-defined for these activations. A more defensible framing comes from borrowing the idea of renormalization group fixed points from physics: features might stabilize at a particular coarse-graining scale not because they're metaphysically atomic but because they're the natural units at which causal interventions produce clean, context-invariant effects — this is implicit in how Anthropic researchers talk about "human-interpretable" as a practical proxy for atomicity, but it smuggles in a human-scale resolution bias. The uncomfortable implication for probing classifier reliability is that if atomicity is scale-relative, then any probe trained at a fixed layer is implicitly operating at an arbitrary causal resolution, and claims like "the model represents X at layer N" are only meaningful relative to an unspecified and unjustified choice of feature granularity — a problem that compounds with depth since middle layers may require finer-grained dictionaries than early or late layers to achieve equivalent causal closure.

The compositional interpretation is plausible but requires distinguishing two very different computational regimes that produce identical splitting signatures: assembly (coarse features from early layers are combined to construct finer features in middle layers) versus disambiguation (a coarse feature that was context-underdetermined early becomes context-specialized later, splitting not because new information was composed but because ambiguity was resolved via attention over prior context). Elhage et al.'s induction head work (2022) and subsequent circuit analyses suggest both happen, often in adjacent layers, which means raw splitting directionality alone cannot distinguish them without tracking which earlier features contribute to the split children — a question that requires cross-layer causal tracing, not just per-layer SAE comparison. The most concrete attempt to reconstruct causal graphs from SAE features is Marks et al. (2024) on sparse feature circuits, where they identify edges between features across layers by measuring how ablating a source feature changes the activation of a target feature, weighted by downstream logit effect — this produces interpretable subgraphs for constrained tasks like indirect object identification, but the graphs are task-conditioned and sparse by construction, meaning they reflect the causal structure of a specific prompt distribution rather than the model's general computational anatomy. The scaling problem is severe: if a middle layer requires a 500K-feature dictionary for causal closure and each feature potentially edges to thousands of features in adjacent layers, the full causal graph has on the order of 10^11 edges for a single layer pair in a large model, making exhaustive reconstruction intractable without strong sparsity assumptions that may not hold. What experts find most epistemically troubling is that the directionality of splitting is not guaranteed to be feedforward — residual stream architecture means a "child" feature in layer N+3 can influence what looks like its "parent" in layer N+1 via attention heads that read far-back positions, so the causal graph may contain cycles or long-range skip connections that make the assembly metaphor actively misleading.

The minimum bar for "general computational primitive" requires at least three independent checks: distributional transfer (the circuit's edges and nodes remain causally active across prompt distributions that share the abstract computation but vary surface form), lesion necessity (ablating the circuit degrades performance on all distributions that require the computation, not just the discovery distribution), and composition reuse (the same subgraph appears as a component in circuits discovered for structurally related but distinct tasks). Wang et al. (2022) on the IOI circuit in GPT-2 small partially attempted the first check by testing across name variations, but the circuit was identified on a highly constrained template, and Variengien & Winsor (2023) later showed that apparently universal "name mover heads" behave differently under paraphrase, suggesting the original circuit was partially epiphenomenal to the specific syntactic form. The strongest positive evidence for a genuine primitive would come from convergent discovery across models: if two models trained with different architectures, data orders, or random seeds independently develop circuits with isomorphic causal graphs for the same abstract computation, the probability that both are epiphenomenal artifacts of a shared prompt distribution is low — this logic underlies Olah et al.'s curve detector universality claims (2020), though those were in vision models with far simpler feature geometry than transformer middle layers. A practical operationalization is minimum description length of the circuit relative to task performance variance: a genuine primitive should explain a disproportionate share of cross-distribution performance variance with a compact causal graph, whereas an epiphenomenal pattern requires ever-more-complex edge additions to cover new distributions — but no one has implemented this as a formal circuit evaluation criterion. The deepest problem is that "general computational primitive" may itself be gradient: a circuit could be genuinely reused across 80% of a task's natural distribution while being supplemented or replaced by parallel circuits in the remaining 20%, making binary classification as primitive versus epiphenomenal a false dichotomy that obscures the model's actual redundant, overlapping computational strategy.

The distinction between deliberate robustness and accidental overparameterization is partly a false dichotomy — training dynamics don't "decide" to be robust, but gradient descent on a sufficiently diverse loss landscape will organically favor redundant solutions because they sit in wider loss basins, which is itself a form of implicit regularization toward robustness without any explicit objective encoding it. The most concrete evidence for robustness-as-training-artifact comes from dropout and noise-injection experiments: models trained with activation dropout develop more parallel circuits for the same computation than models trained cleanly (Morcos et al. 2018 on representation similarity under ablation), suggesting redundancy tracks the stochasticity of the training signal rather than an independent robustness objective — which is consistent with accidental overparameterization being the proximate cause, with robustness as a downstream consequence. A potentially distinguishing observable is ablation complementarity: if redundancy is robustness-functional, ablating one circuit should cause the other to upregulate or increase its causal contribution (compensatory engagement), whereas if redundancy is accidental, ablating one circuit should leave the other's contribution unchanged since there was no learned coupling between them — Meyes et al. and related ablation studies have found mixed evidence, with some head groups showing compensation and others showing independence, suggesting both origins coexist within the same model. A second observable is the correlation between redundancy degree and training distribution tail coverage: genuine robustness circuits should be redundant specifically for inputs near the decision boundary or in low-frequency regions of the training distribution, whereas accidental redundancy should be uniformly distributed across input space — no one has cleanly tested this prediction at the circuit level, though it's implicit in work on shortcut learning where tail-distribution performance collapses under ablation in ways that bulk performance does not. The sharpest expert worry is that even if you could conclusively show redundancy is accidental in origin, it becomes functionally indistinguishable from robustness after sufficient training — the model has been selected for outputs, not mechanisms, so accidental redundancy that happens to improve generalization will be preserved by gradient descent regardless of its origin, making the causal history of the circuit unrecoverable from its current structure alone.

Yes, mechanistic interpretability findings are inherently synchronic — they describe the current computational structure without recovering the developmental trajectory that produced it, and this is not merely a technical limitation but a fundamental consequence of the fact that gradient descent is a lossy compression of training history into weights. The alignment-relevant question is whether synchronic descriptions are sufficient for the use cases that matter: detecting deceptive alignment, verifying that a model won't generalize dangerously out of distribution, or confirming that a safety-relevant concept is robustly represented. For deceptive alignment detection specifically, the historical limitation matters critically — a model that learned an alignment-relevant behavior through a robust causal circuit versus one that learned a superficially identical behavior through a brittle shortcut may be indistinguishable by current circuit analysis, yet have radically different out-of-distribution behavior, exactly the failure mode Evan Hubinger et al. (2019) identified in the sleeper agent framing. The limitation matters less for some alignment uses than others: if the goal is simply to verify that a specific dangerous capability (e.g., bioweapon synthesis routing) is absent from the current model's circuits, synchronic analysis may be sufficient — you don't need to know why it's absent to confirm it is, modulo the circuit completeness problem. What experts find most troubling is the generalization gap: circuit analysis is necessarily performed on finite prompt distributions, but alignment failures by definition occur in novel distributions, and a synchronic description cannot distinguish a circuit that will generalize safely from one that will fracture — Anthropic's model organisms of misalignment work (2024) demonstrated that behaviorally aligned models can harbor dormant misaligned circuits invisible to behavioral testing, and there's no current interpretability method that reliably detects dormancy versus absence.
